title: What Can Learn from PER: Physics Education Research?
extended_summary:
This paper is a practitioner-oriented overview of Physics Education Research (PER) and what it suggests about effective physics teaching. It does not report a new empirical study; instead, it summarizes research-based instructional principles that instructors can use to improve learning in physics. The piece is written as guidance for new teachers and frames PER as a body of evidence about how students learn physics at all levels.

The central message is that students learn best through interactive engagement rather than passive listening. The paper highlights several PER-supported ideas: students should actively construct understanding, work in small groups with appropriate instructor support, build on their prior knowledge, learn through well-defined goals and aligned assessment, and receive instruction that helps them transfer ideas across contexts. It also emphasizes the importance of student buy-in and of explaining why struggle and active learning are part of effective instruction.

The intended population is broad physics instruction, especially introductory undergraduate physics, and the setting is classroom-based teaching. The article concludes that PER-based approaches are generally student-centered, can be adapted to local constraints, and are particularly helpful for underrepresented students by narrowing achievement gaps. Because the article is a synthesis/position piece rather than a causal comparison study, it does not provide primary evidence on delayed post-tests, transfer tasks, subgroup effects, or implementation fidelity beyond general guidance.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative, theory-oriented overview article in physics education, not a causal comparison study and not an AI-powered K-12 science intervention study. It does not report an empirical design, sample, or outcome analysis for the requested target domain.
impact_tier_rationale: No evaluative evidence is reported for AI tools, delayed post-tests, transfer tasks, subgroup effects, or implementation fidelity. The paper offers general pedagogical claims from PER, but it does not support the optimistic thesis for AI-powered K-12 science causal comparison studies because it is outside the target evidence base.
